title: How much caffeine is in cocoa?

seo.title: How much caffeine is in cocoa? Real serving amounts
seo.meta_description: Cocoa does contain caffeine, but usually much less per mug than coffee. See how much is in a tablespoon and why natural and Dutch cocoa can differ.
seo.search_intent: Find how much caffeine cocoa powder provides in a normal serving

excerpt: Cocoa powder does contain caffeine. The USDA unsweetened natural cocoa reference has 230 mg per 100 g, about 12 mg in a 5.4 g tablespoon. A USDA alkalized cocoa entry is much lower, illustrating how widely products can vary. Theobromine, not caffeine, is cocoa's dominant methylxanthine.
content_html:
Cocoa is not naturally decaffeinated. It contains caffeine, but the amount in a spoonful is usually much smaller than the amount in a cup of coffee. Per-100-gram numbers can make cocoa look more caffeinated than the serving actually is.

How much is in a tablespoon?

The USDA Standard Reference entry for natural unsweetened cocoa powder lists about 230 mg caffeine per 100 g. Its household measure puts one tablespoon at about 5.4 g, which works out to roughly 12 mg caffeine.

Natural cocoa amountApprox. caffeine
5 g~12 mg
10 g~23 mg
20 g~46 mg

Those are scale-setting calculations, not guaranteed values for every brand. A separate USDA entry for cocoa processed with alkali lists only about 78 mg/100 g, showing how much processing and source material can matter.

Why cocoa caffeine varies

Cocoa variety, origin, fermentation, roasting, and downstream processing all affect methylxanthines. A cocoa drink mix adds another variable: if only part of the powder is cocoa, each gram of the mix contains less cocoa-derived caffeine than a gram of 100% cocoa.

Theobromine is much more abundant

Cocoa's dominant methylxanthine is theobromine. The same USDA natural-cocoa entry contains about 2,057 mg theobromine per 100 g, almost nine times its caffeine level. A 5.4 g tablespoon would provide roughly 111 mg.

Theobromine and caffeine are related compounds, but they do not have identical potency or effects. Their milligrams should not be added together as though they were caffeine equivalents.

How cocoa compares with coffee

EFSA uses rough guide values of 90 mg caffeine in a 200 mL cup of filter coffee and 80 mg in a 60 mL espresso. A drink made with 5–10 g of the USDA natural cocoa reference would contribute about 12–23 mg from the cocoa.

A 50 g bar of dark chocolate is listed by EFSA at roughly 25 mg as a broad guide, though cacao percentage and recipe change the number.

Does cocoa at night matter?

It can if you are sensitive. Some people notice small doses; others do not. The total also includes coffee, tea, soda, energy drinks, chocolate, and medications or supplements that may contain caffeine.

The useful takeaway is simply that cocoa is low-caffeine relative to coffee by normal serving size, not caffeine-free.

faq.question: How much caffeine is in one tablespoon of cocoa powder?
faq.answer: About 12 mg using the USDA natural unsweetened cocoa reference and its 5.4 g tablespoon measure. Other cocoa powders can differ substantially.

faq.question: Does cocoa have more caffeine than coffee?
faq.answer: Usually not per serving. A 200 mL filter coffee is about 90 mg in EFSA's guide, versus roughly 12–23 mg from 5–10 g of the natural cocoa reference.

faq.question: Does Dutch-process cocoa have less caffeine?
faq.answer: It can. The USDA alkalized entry cited here has 78 mg/100 g versus 230 mg/100 g for natural cocoa, but that ratio should not be assumed for every brand.

faq.question: What is theobromine?
faq.answer: It is another methylxanthine in cocoa and is present in much larger amounts than caffeine. Its effects are not identical to caffeine's.
